subject: physics
question_text: What is the contribution of S. Chandrasekhar to Physics?

mark_split.label: The value and what it means

verification.note: Asked in TS Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I, March 2019 (Q1), March 2023 (Q1) and March 2025 (Q1) — Section A, 2 marks each time. The 2023 paper prints the name as "S. Chandra Sekhar", the same question with a board typo. The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question text itself is sourced from those papers. `appearances` is deliberately left empty — a separate reviewed tagging pass fills it, and a hand-written tag here would be an invented claim. Content hand-checked against NCERT Class-11 Chapter 1: S. Chandrasekhar's contribution is the Chandrasekhar limit, the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf star, about 1.4 solar masses; he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1983.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The Chandrasekhar limit
lines: S. Chandrasekhar worked on the structure
and evolution of stars. His contribution
is the Chandrasekhar limit: the largest
mass a stable white dwarf star can have.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The words maximum mass and white dwarf are both checked.
steps.why: A white dwarf is held up against its own gravity by the pressure of its electrons. That pressure has an upper limit, so above a certain mass it is no longer enough to support the star.
common_mistakes: Saying the limit is the maximum mass of any star. It is the maximum mass of a stable WHITE DWARF.

recall.must_convey: That S Chandrasekhar gave the Chandrasekhar limit, the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf star.
accept: maximum mass of a white dwarf

steps.memory_tip: The Chandrasekhar limit is a MASS, and it belongs to white dwarf stars only.

steps.margin_note: Second mark. The number 1.4 together with the words solar masses.
steps.why: The number is what makes the limit useful, because it sorts the end states of stars: below about 1.4 solar masses a star ends as a white dwarf, and above it the collapse continues.
common_mistakes: Writing 1.4 kg or 1.4 × 10³⁰ kg without saying solar masses.
Giving the limit as 1.4 times the mass of the earth.

recall.must_convey: That the limit is about 1.4 solar masses, and a heavier star cannot stay a white dwarf.
accept: 1.4 times the mass of the sun
heavier star cannot be a white dwarf

steps.memory_tip: One point four suns. Under the limit, a white dwarf; over it, the collapse goes on.

insider_note: Name the limit and give 1.4 solar masses — the name with no number, or the number with no name, is one mark of the two.
